correctness.rationale: For three candidates without pairwise ties, the Kemeny correspondence is determined by the majority tournament: a transitive tournament yields its Condorcet winner, while a cycle yields the candidate defeated on a minimum-margin edge, uniquely when that edge is uniquely weakest. Odd electorates give odd margins, so every strict positive-margin gap is at least two. A unilateral report changes each pairwise margin by at most two, and a voter sincerely preferring the target candidate already supports the target against the truthful winner. The complete case analysis therefore rules out a preferred singleton endpoint. Two independent Kemeny implementations agree on every anonymous odd-electorate profile through seventeen voters and find zero profitable singleton-to-singleton changes.

originality.rationale: The closest prior work classifies strategic Kemeny boundaries for three candidates, including the fact that manipulable boundaries separate rankings at Kendall distance two. The new claim is narrower in tie treatment but sharper in endpoint structure: for odd electorates no profitable unilateral move can have singleton Kemeny winner sets at both endpoints. The inspected sources and targeted semantic searches did not state this parity-based localization result.
residual_risks: The detailed strategic-voter table in Wang-Cuff-Kulkarni is close prior art and may make the new theorem derivable as an unstated discrete corollary.
An unindexed voting-theory note or treatment of the equivalent three-candidate maximin rule may state the singleton-endpoint property explicitly.
The theorem does not address even electorates, arbitrary resolute tie-breaking at tied correspondence profiles, coalitional manipulation, or four or more candidates.

value.rationale: Kemeny-Young is a canonical Condorcet method, and manipulation is a central design concern. The theorem localizes every profitable unilateral manipulation in odd three-candidate electorates to the tie locus of the underlying Kemeny correspondence. This is a structural explanation—based on the exact two-unit ballot effect and odd-margin spacing—of why tie handling is indispensable in the smallest nontrivial Kemeny incentive problem, rather than a routine finite census.
